title: Prompt-injection-aware tooling
subtitle: Tool descriptions are attack surface. Shell-template injection fixtures are mandatory for the tool kind that needs them, and the discovery tool's description is capped by a test.

stats.label: tool descriptions treated as untrusted text
servers whose catalogs are read, never called

lede: In FAFOHive I wanted readable guides to every tool across its servers, most of them published by vendors. Asking a model to summarise each tool has a trap in it: a tool's name, description and schema are text written by whoever published the tool, and a model that reads them with any authority can be steered by them. I decided every tool description is untrusted data and built a tool explorer around that. Discovery is read-only. The explorer reads each server's catalog and never calls a tool, so exploring cannot cause a side effect. Official descriptions and AI-written guides are stored and shown separately and never merge, so a reader always knows which one they are reading.
quote: I build AI features on the assumption that model inputs can be hostile: the model gets text without trust, and its output is checked against facts it could not forge.
evidence: Prompt-injection defence: about 500 tool descriptions treated as untrusted data, read from the catalogs of 3 servers and never called during discovery.
LLM output verification: AI-written tool guides keyed to a SHA-256 hash of each tool, in batches rejected whole on one forged identifier, duplicate entry or mismatched hash.
Sandboxed model sessions: audits that start only when I start them, in a locked-down command-line session that can write nothing but its output file.
author: Corey James
